items.mnemonic_text: Two bent bows losing their tension: weak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, an archer draws her <radical>bow</radical>, but overnight <radical>ice</radical> has crept along the wood, gluing the string stiff against the frame. She hauls back and the string only creaks, then sags loose the instant she lets go — the arrow drops dead at her own boots. <kanji>Weak</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Halfway down that same icy trail, a hiker named <reading>Jock</reading> collapses against a boulder, legs shaking, and moans <reading>じゃく</reading>, じゃく, over and over. The frozen bow slides out of his numb fingers into the snow.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は体が弱いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は体[からだ]が弱[よわ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の声はとても弱いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の声[こえ]はとても弱[よわ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は病気で弱くなりました。
example_sentences.english: He became weak because of his illness.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は病[びょう]気[き]で弱[よわ]くなりました。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) hidden behind sound (音) of night: dark.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the little <radical>sun</radical> behind its two-bar window is just climbing to start the day. The biggest cat on the steps rears onto its hind legs to <radical>stand</radical> in the doorway, paws braced wide like it owns the place. Its shadow swallows the whole window in one go, and the mossy steps drop into <kanji>dark</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane fumbles for the huge bell in the sudden dark and rings it anyway. From behind the cat, a startled visitor named <reading>Anne</reading> gasps <reading>あん</reading>, あん — can't see a thing — groping past fur to find the steps.

example_sentences.japanese: 外はもう暗いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 外[そと]はもう暗[くら]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 空が暗くなりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 空[そら]が暗[くら]くなりました。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は暗くて狭いです。
example_sentences.english: This room is dark and cramped.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は暗[くら]くて狭[せま]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Drops falling inside a window frame from the sky: rain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look through the window frame and watch the <radical>rain</radical> falling inside it, one drop after another down the glass. Those little drops caught in the frame are all you need to picture. Drops falling inside a window frame: that's <kanji>rain</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow gets caught outside in the downpour and lets out a long, miserable "<reading>う</reading>ー" as the drops soak her. Every time it rains, that cow's soggy うー is the sound you hear.
items.description: Means "rain"; the base kanji for weather words and it sits on top of many other weather-related characters as a component.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日はたくさん雨が降りました。
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]はたくさん雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は雨が嫌いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は雨[あめ]が嫌[きら]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は雨ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: A slash over ten (十) multiplies it into a thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take the plus sign for <radical>ten</radical> and lay a single slash across its top, like one bold pen-stroke scratched over it. That one extra mark turns humble ten into something enormous — you've just multiplied it a hundredfold. Ten with a lid on top means a <kanji>thousand</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A senator named Sen shows up at the shrine and drops a thousand coins into the offering box all at once. "That's from all my constituents," she says, "<reading>せん</reading> of them exactly." Every time you see this kanji, hear Sen bragging about her せん coins.
items.description: Count the horizontals and look at the top. 千 has one bar under a slanting flick. 十 has one bar and no flick, just a straight cross. 午 and 干 both carry two bars — 午 under a flick, 干 starting flat.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から千まで書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote from one to one thousand.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から千[せん]まで書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が千人来ました。
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が千[せん]人[にん]来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 千の魚を見ました。
example_sentences.furigana: 千[せん]の魚[さかな]を見[み]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone sweeps the yard with a <radical>broom</radical>, one <radical>slide</radical> of a stroke clearing the <radical>ground</radical>. He opens his <radical>mouth</radical> with tomorrow's orders: not the emperor, just the man above you, <kanji>mister</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kun is the teacher who refuses to use first names. Every boy in the class gets the same syllable barked after his surname — 「<reading>くん</reading>」 — as the seating chart comes out. Tanaka-くん. Sato-くん. It is how you know he means you.

items.mnemonic_text: A dog (犬) squeezing back under a door (戸): to return.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That raccoon that rammed through the <radical>door</radical>, scraping its tail on the sill as it barreled into the kitchen, doesn't stop there. It circles the block, and twenty minutes later barges back through that same battered door, right where it started, tail scraping the sill all over again. That's <kanji>return</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Next door, a neighbor named Ray sighs <reading>れい</reading> every time he hears the door bang, flat and resigned, like counting the raccoon's laps with a low '<reading>ray</reading>'. Sure enough, a beat later, it barrels back through, right on cue.
items.description: This kanji's on'yomi is genuinely rare in modern Japanese. Outside a handful of fixed compounds, it overwhelmingly appears with its kun'yomi reading instead, so lean on that reading first in real text you encounter.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, shoved to the back with <radical>rice</radical> and something <radical>big</radical> on top. You walk through every room to reach it; nobody outside the family does. The deepest room is the <kanji>heart</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

items.mnemonic_text: Grass on top of a person changing (化): a blooming flower.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A fresh patch of <radical>grass</radical> sprouts from the soil, two clumps poking up over one line of dirt. This morning, one clump goes rogue. It shoots a stem straight up, a wide bloom spilling open at the end. The rest of the grass sits underneath, looking embarrassed. Grass with a blossom bursting from the top — that's a <kanji>flower</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands right in the middle of the flowerbed and lets out a proud 「<reading>か</reading>」, singeing every petal within reach. Now the only flower left standing is the scorched one under her claws.
items.description: Means "flower"; a very common everyday kanji seen in words for flowers, plants, and blossoms.

example_sentences.japanese: 母に花を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought flowers for my mother.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]に花[はな]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で花を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw flowers at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で花[はな]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この花は高いです。
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は高[たか]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, above her a <radical>broom</radical> on its <radical>stick</radical>, <radical>ground</radical> ruled across top. Not sweeping somebody's house — the broom, floor, roof are hers: the <kanji>wife</kanji> running them.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) waiting where trains stop: a station.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You're waiting on the platform when a galloping <radical>horse</radical> thunders past you onto the tracks. It has to hurdle a <radical>body</radical> sprawled across the bench — the same commuter who faceplanted hours ago. The conductor just sighs. Horses on the rails, sleepers on the benches: where else but the <kanji>station</kanji>?
items.reading_mnemonic: A commuter named Eki misses the last train and shouts "<reading>えき</reading>! えき!" across the empty platform, hoping the station master will hear her and hold the doors.
items.description: Means "station" — the word for a train or subway station, seen constantly in place names and on transit signs.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は家から近いです。
example_sentences.english: The station is close to my house.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は家[いえ]から近[ちか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員に切符を見せます。
example_sentences.english: I show my ticket to the station staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]に切[きっ]符[ぷ]を見[み]せます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝この駅で電車に乗ります。
example_sentences.english: I board the train at this station every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]この駅[えき]で電[でん]車[しゃ]に乗[の]ります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> across the top, under a <radical>person</radical> kneeling on bare <radical>ground</radical> as the clerk presses her <radical>stamp</radical> on the ledger. It lands where the crop should count, printing a round <kanji>zero</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> stands at the left, beside the shape of <radical>stopping</radical>: an eye that has seen something, a foot that will not move. She is planted in the doorway, arms folded — not going out tonight. Somebody's <kanji>daughter</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」. It is the address for a girl of good family who is not allowed out tonight. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) not yet (未) grown: the younger sister.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the same crossed-limbed <radical>woman</radical> turns up tangled sideways in a <radical>tree</radical>, arms still flung wide. She giggles, refusing to climb down until someone catches her. That reckless, easily rescued climber is your <kanji>younger sister</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Below her, someone shouts that she'll fall, and all she yells back, upside down and gleeful, is a stretched-out <reading>まい</reading> — <reading>my</reading> turn, not yet! — before slipping another branch lower.
items.description: Don't confuse this with 姉, the kanji for older sister. Here the right side is a tree with an extra short stroke near the top, giving two branches instead of one. The right side of 姉 instead stacks a lid over a hanging fold of cloth, a cap over drapery. Two branches is younger; cap-over-cloth is older.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は毎朝六時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister gets up at six every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]六[ろく]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は魚が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は魚[さかな]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は公園で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister reads a book in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は公[こう]園[えん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A dangling shape on the side of the head: an ear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you'll spot a dangling <radical>ear</radical> shape hanging off the side of a head. That soft, drooping flap catching every sound is an <kanji>ear</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A jittery DJ named Jiji cups a hand to his ear and shouts "<reading>じ</reading>, じ, do you hear that beat?" — the sound goes straight into his ear as じ.
items.description: Means "ear"; the body part, and shows up in words about hearing and listening.

example_sentences.japanese: あの犬は耳が大きいです。
example_sentences.furigana: あの犬[いぬ]は耳[みみ]が大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの耳は小さいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの耳[みみ]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 耳が冷たいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 耳[みみ]が冷[つめ]たいです。

items.mnemonic_text: A dying (亡) heart (心) losing its memory: to forget.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the wounded, thumping <radical>heart</radical> — hook dragging low, three drops flung off the barb — snags on a locker door and stops, mid-beat. Whatever it was carrying drains out through the hook, like the blood has. By the time it works loose and wobbles on, it cannot recall what it snagged on. That blank, drained heart is <kanji>forgetting</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down the empty hallway, a ghost named <reading>Bo</reading> drifts past the snagged heart and moans <reading>ぼう</reading>, hollow. It's the exact sound of something that used to matter, fading out of a heart's grip entirely.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日、宿題を忘れました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を忘[わす]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも名前を忘れます。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はいつも名[な]前[まえ]を忘[わす]れます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは約束を忘れませんでした。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは約[やく]束[そく]を忘[わす]れませんでした。

items.mnemonic_text: Horns flaring above a frame of stiff crossed legs: a sheep.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape and you'll find nothing new in it: two short strokes flaring out at the top like horns, and a frame beneath locked into four stiff crossed legs. Not one stroke has been added to the <radical>sheep</radical> you already know. Standing on its own, unchanged, it is simply a <kanji>sheep</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The flock's leader shoulders through the door of Koichi's konbini like a regular, and Koichi barely glances up before giving it the usual greeting: "<reading>よう</reading>!" The sheep bleats it straight back at him, <reading>よう</reading>, and heads for the onigiri shelf.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山に白い羊がたくさんいます。
example_sentences.english: There are a lot of white sheep on that mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]に白[しろ]い羊[ひつじ]がたくさんいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昼ご飯に羊の肉を食べました。
example_sentences.furigana: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]に羊[ひつじ]の肉[にく]を食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 羊が道の真ん中に立っています。
example_sentences.english: A sheep is standing in the middle of the road.
example_sentences.furigana: 羊[ひつじ]が道[みち]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に立[た]っています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> on the left, beside it the <radical>small</radical> mark — one bristle off the very top, thinnest thing on the plant. Slice an hour the same way and the sliver left in your hand is one <kanji>second</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the far left, beside him a <radical>big</radical> load: a <radical>sheep</radical> he must carry in. He <radical>splits</radical> it for everyone else before he eats — the humble word he uses for <kanji>me</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.
